1.q: אִם־יַעֲמֹ֨ד מֹשֶׁ֤ה וּ⁠שְׁמוּאֵל֙ לְ⁠פָנַ֔⁠י אֵ֥ין נַפְשִׁ֖⁠י אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
1.note: Yahweh is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. **Moses** and **Samuel** had died long before this time, so they could not stand before him and plead for the people. He is stating it as a condition to show that any willingness on his part to spare **this people** is also not true. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, I still would not feel favorable toward this people]

The implication is that **Moses** and **Samuel** were remembered as men whose prayers had turned Yahweh’s anger away from the people in the past. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [If Moses and Samuel, who prayed for this people long ago, stood to my face]
Here, **my face** represents my presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before me]

Yahweh is using **my soul would not {be} to this people** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I would not show favor to this people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would not be favorably disposed toward this people]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:7.

2.q: כִּֽי־יֹאמְר֥וּ אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ אָ֣נָה נֵצֵ֑א וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֨ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֜ם כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה
2.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [if they say to you, ‘Where should we go?’ Then you shall tell them that Yahweh has said that]

This could mean: (1) the people might ask Jeremiah where they should go. Alternate translation: [perhaps they they say to you, ‘Where should we go] or (2) at some time, the people really will ask Jeremiah where they should go. Alternate translation: [when they say to you, ‘Where should we go]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Judah in general, not to specific people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [if the people say to you] or [if you are asked]

Yahweh uses a repetitive series of clauses to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

Here, **the sword** represents death in war. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for death in battle to death in battle]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for being taken away as captives to being taken away as captives.”]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5. This also occurs in verse 19 of this chapter.

3.note: The implication is that these **four kinds** are four kinds of destroyers, which Yahweh names in the rest of this verse. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [four kinds of destroyers]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 6, 9, and 20.

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will appoint the sword to kill them, and I will appoint the dogs to drag away their corpses, and I will appoint the bird of the skies and the beast of the earth to devour and to destroy them]

Here, **the sword** represents enemy soldiers armed with swords. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Enemy soldiers with swords to kill]

In this verse, the words **bird** and **beast** are singular in form, but they refer to all birds and all wild animals as groups. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of “bird” and “beast.” Alternate translation: [and the birds of the skies and the beasts of the earth]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something terrifying]

The implication is that **what he did in Jerusalem** refers to the wicked things that **Manasseh** did there, especially setting up idols and shedding innocent blood. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the wicked things he did in Jerusalem]

5.q: כִּ֠י מִֽי־יַחְמֹ֤ל עָלַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וּ⁠מִ֖י יָנ֣וּד לָ֑⁠ךְ וּ⁠מִ֣י יָס֔וּר לִ⁠שְׁאֹ֥ל לְ⁠שָׁלֹ֖ם לָֽ⁠ךְ
5.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one at all will pity the people of Jerusalem or mourn for them or care how they are doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one will have compassion on you, Jerusalem, and no one will grieve for you, and no one will turn aside to ask about your well-being!]

Here, **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [inhabitants of Jerusalem]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **well-being**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how you are doing]

6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s turning away from him were a matter of walking **backward**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have rejected me]

Yahweh is using **stretch out my hand against you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “attack you and harm you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [therefore I will attack you and harm you]

Yahweh is using **weary of relenting** as a common expression of the culture to mean “tired of slackening.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am no longer willing to hold back from punishing you]

7.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **winnow** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And I will thoroughly winnow them]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people were grain that he would **winnow** and scatter away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will drive them away in the gates of the land]

A **winnowing fork** is a kind of farming tool with long prongs that a worker used to throw threshed grain into the air so that the wind would blow the chaff away. If your readers would not be familiar with what a winnowing fork is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with a pitchfork]

Here, **the gates** represents the towns and cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the towns and cities of the land]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **turn back**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [since they keep going the same evil ways]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people’s conduct were **ways**, that is, paths that they walk on, and as if changing that conduct were a matter of **turn**ing around and going the other direction. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [{since} they refuse to abandon their evil conduct]

8.note: Jeremiah says **Their widows will be numerous to me, more than the sand of the seas** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [There will be very many widows]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sand of the seas** is too plentiful for anyone to count, so the **widows** among the people will be too many to number. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Their widows will be so numerous to me that no one will be able to count them]

The phrase **to me** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [before me]

The implication is that **the mother of the young men** refers to the many mothers who will lose their young men when the enemy attacks. Alternate translation: [against the mothers whose young men will die]

The implication is that **at the noonday** means that the attack will come in broad daylight, at a time when the people would not expect it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in broad daylight, when they do not expect an attack]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anguish** and **terror**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [I will cause the women to suddenly feel anguished and terrified]

The pronoun **her** refers to the mothers whom Yahweh has just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will cause anguish and terror to fall on those mothers suddenly]

9.note: The implication is that a woman who had borne **seven** sons had a complete and secure family, so this describes someone who had every reason to feel safe. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The woman who had borne seven sons and whose family seemed complete and secure]

Yahweh is using **breathe out her life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “gasp for breath and die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [She will gasp for breath and die]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the ending of this woman’s life and hope were a day in which the **sun** goes down long before evening. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Her life will end while she is still young]

The terms **ashamed** and **disgraced** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [She will be utterly humiliated]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Judah, not to the woman whom Yahweh has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the remnant of the people of Judah]

10.note: Here the speaker changes from Yahweh to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating a change of speaker in your language. Alternate translation: [And then Jeremiah responded.]

Jeremiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief and distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How miserable I am, my mother, that you bore me]

Jeremiah is using **a man of strife and a man of contention** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a person whom everyone quarrels with and opposes.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a source of quarreling and opposition]

The terms **a man of strife** and **a man of contention** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a man with whom everyone argues and fights]

Here, **the land** represents the people who live in the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to everyone living in the land]

The implication is that lending and borrowing money regularly led to quarrels, so Jeremiah is saying that he has given the people no such reason to oppose him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I have given no one reason to quarrel with me, for I have not lent money to anyone, nor has anyone lent money to me]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people of the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but every one of the people of the land is cursing me]

11.note: The phrase **Surely I have loosened you for good** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense in this context. Scholars have proposed that the ancient Greek translation preserves the original wording here, which results in the following alternate translation. You may want to follow the ULT or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Surely I will strengthen you for good]

The terms **the time of disaster** and **the time of distress** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in the time of terrible calamity]

12.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to break **iron** or **bronze**. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can break iron, iron from the north, or bronze!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if a people were **iron** or **bronze** that cannot be broken. This could mean (1) the invading army from the north, which the people of Judah will not be able to withstand. Alternate translation: [the strong army that comes from the north] or (2) the stubbornness of the people of Judah, which they themselves cannot break. Alternate translation: [a people stubborn and hard as iron in battle with an enemy like iron from the north, or bronze]

13.note: The pronoun **Your** refers to the people of Judah here, not to Jeremiah, whom Yahweh has been addressing in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The wealth and treasures of you people of Judah]

13.q: לָ⁠בַ֥ז אֶתֵּ֖ן לֹ֣א בִ⁠מְחִ֑יר וּ⁠בְ⁠כָל־חַטֹּאותֶ֖י⁠ךָ וּ⁠בְ⁠כָל־גְּבוּלֶֽי⁠ךָ
13.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **throughout your territories** with the information about giving your wealth **for plunder**. Alternate translation: [I will give for plunder throughout your territories, with no price, because of all your sins]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sins**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of everything you have done wrong]

14.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “Then I will cause your enemies to bring you into a land that you do not know.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Then I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Yahweh is using **a fire is kindled in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I have become very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Your culture may also associate anger with heat or with a particular part of the body, and if so, you could use its characteristic expression in your translation. Alternate translation: [I have become very angry, and my anger shall consume you.”]

The expression **is kindled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I have kindled a fire in my nose]

15.note: Here the speaker changes from Yahweh to Jeremiah, who is now praying to Yahweh, although the text does not say so. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating a change of speaker in your language. Alternate translation: [And Jeremiah responded,]

The implication is that Jeremiah wants Yahweh to acknowledge what he is suffering from the people who oppose him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you yourself know what I am suffering]

The words translated as **Remember**, **visit**, and **take vengeance** are imperatives, but they communicate a request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [I ask you to remember me, and I beg you to come to me and avenge me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and avenge me on the ones persecuting me]

Jeremiah is using **the length of your nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “your patience in not becoming angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Please do not let me die while you patiently withhold your anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [others insult me because of you]

16.note: The expression **were found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I found your words]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s words were food that he **ate**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I gladly received what you said]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **joy** and **rejoicing**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [delightful to me and made my heart rejoice]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if his feelings were located in his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my inmost self rejoiced]

Jeremiah is using **by your name I am called** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I belong to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for I am yours]

The expression **I am called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [you have called me by your name]

17.note: Here, **your hand** represents your power that compelled me. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [because of your compelling power]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if he were a container that Yahweh had **filled** with anger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have caused me to be very indignant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **indignation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with what makes me indignant]

18.q: לָ֣⁠מָּה הָיָ֤ה כְאֵבִ⁠י֙ נֶ֔צַח וּ⁠מַכָּתִ֖⁠י אֲנוּשָׁ֑ה֙ מֵֽאֲנָה֙ הֵֽרָפֵ֔א
18.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to complain that his suffering never comes to an end. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My pain is endless and my wound is incurable, refusing to be healed!]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if his suffering were a **wound** that no one is able to heal. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my suffering permanent]

The expression **to be healed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [refusing to heal]

Jeremiah is speaking of his **wound** as if it were a living thing that could refuse to get better. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [never getting better]

18.q: הָי֨וֹ תִֽהְיֶ֥ה לִ⁠י֙ כְּמ֣וֹ אַכְזָ֔ב מַ֖יִם לֹ֥א נֶאֱמָֽנוּ
18.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to accuse Yahweh of failing him when he needs help. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have become to me like a deceptive brook, like unreliable waters!]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **deceptive {brook}** is unreliable and may fail a traveler who needs water, so Yahweh seems to Jeremiah to be unreliable and to fail him when he needs help. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [unreliable, like a brook that fails a thirsty traveler when he needs it, like waters that a person cannot depend upon]

19.q: אִם־תָּשׁ֤וּב וַ⁠אֲשִֽׁיבְ⁠ךָ֙ לְ⁠פָנַ֣⁠י תַּֽעֲמֹ֔ד וְ⁠אִם־תּוֹצִ֥יא יָקָ֛ר מִ⁠זּוֹלֵ֖ל כְּ⁠פִ֣⁠י תִֽהְיֶ֑ה יָשֻׁ֤בוּ הֵ֨מָּה֙ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אַתָּ֖ה לֹֽא־תָשׁ֥וּב אֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
19.note: In this verse Yahweh repeats a single word from the original language in several different senses, “return,” “restore,” and “turn.” This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Jeremiah’s repenting were a physical **return** to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you turn back from your sin]

Yahweh is using **stand to my face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “serve me as my prophet.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you shall serve me as my prophet]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Jeremiah’s speech were metallic ore from which he could **take out the precious** and leave behind what is **worthless**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And if you speak what is valuable instead of what is worthless]

Yahweh is using the adjective **precious** as a noun to mean “something of great value.” Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [what is precious] or [what is of great value]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person’s **mouth** speaks that person’s own words, so Jeremiah will speak Yahweh’s own words to the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you will speak my own words to them]

19.q: יָשֻׁ֤בוּ הֵ֨מָּה֙ אֵלֶ֔י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אַתָּ֖ה לֹֽא־תָשׁ֥וּב אֲלֵי⁠הֶֽם
19.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if accepting what someone says were a matter of physically turning toward that person, so **They themselves shall turn to you** means that the people would accept what Jeremiah tells them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They themselves shall accept what you say, but you yourself shall not accept what they say]

20.q: וּ⁠נְתַתִּ֜י⁠ךָ לָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה לְ⁠חוֹמַ֤ת נְחֹ֨שֶׁת֙ בְּצוּרָ֔ה
20.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if Jeremiah were **a wall of fortified bronze** that the people could not break through. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make you able to withstand this people, as strong as a fortified bronze wall]

The terms **save** and **deliver** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to certainly rescue you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:19.
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:10.

21.q: וְ⁠הִצַּלְתִּ֖י⁠ךָ מִ⁠יַּ֣ד רָעִ֑ים וּ⁠פְדִתִ֖י⁠ךָ מִ⁠כַּ֥ף עָרִצִֽים
21.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will surely rescue you from the power of wicked and ruthless people]

Here, **the hand** and **the palm** represent “the power and control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of the evil … from the control of the ruthless]

Yahweh is using the adjectives **the evil** and **the ruthless** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who do evil … those who act ruthlessly]
